title: How Saurav Ghosal Mentored 18-Year-Old Anahat Singh to India's First Junior Squash World Title
excerpt: The retired Indian squash great's two-year mentorship helped Anahat Singh break Egypt's 16-year stranglehold on the World Junior Championship, signaling a generational shift in Indian squash ahead of the sport's Olympic debut.
body:
• Anahat Singh, 18, became the first Indian to win the World Junior Squash Championship, defeating Egypt's Ruqayya Salem 3-0 (11-3, 11-7, 11-9) in the final at Niagara-on-the-Lake, Canada.
  • Her victory ended 16 consecutive years of Egyptian dominance in the tournament — she is the first non-Egyptian champion since Amanda Sobhy of the United States in 2010.
  • Retired Indian squash great Saurav Ghosal, who has mentored Singh since 2024, played a pivotal role in reshaping her tactical game and mental approach.
  • With squash set for its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028, Singh — currently ranked world No. 20 — is India's brightest medal prospect in the sport.

A Historic Win in Niagara-on-the-Lake

Anahat Singh walked onto the court in Niagara-on-the-Lake, Canada, knowing two things: this was her final junior tournament, and she had never won the title. Four previous attempts had ended in quarter-final and semi-final exits. Last year, she came closest — a bronze medal after a 3-0 semi-final loss to Egypt's Nadien Elhammamy.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2084107070153134424

On July 26, the Delhi-born 18-year-old made her last chance count. As the top seed, Singh dismantled second-seeded Ruqayya Salem of Egypt in straight games — 11-3, 11-7, 11-9 — to become the first Indian to win a squash world title at any level.

The victory ended Egypt's 16-year monopoly on the women's junior world championship. No non-Egyptian player had won since Amanda Sobhy of the United States in 2010. To get there, Singh defeated three Egyptian opponents across the quarter-finals, semi-finals, and final, beating Barb Sameh and Habiba Rizk before dispatching Salem in the title match.

"I still feel like I am dreaming. This tournament has been like a curse because of my repeated quarter-final and semi-final exits. I knew it was my final opportunity to win the junior title."

— Anahat Singh, after the final

The Ghosal Factor

Behind Singh's tactical evolution stands Saurav Ghosal, the most accomplished Indian squash player in history. Ghosal, who became the first Indian to break into the world's top 10 in 2019 and the first to reach a World Championship quarter-final in 2013, retired from professional play in 2025 after a degenerative hip condition ended his career.

He joined Singh's coaching team in 2024, working alongside French coaches Stephane Galifi and Gregory Gaultier — the latter a former world champion. Where Galifi and Gaultier handle the technical and physical coaching, Ghosal's role has been strategic: helping Singh decide which tournaments to play, reshaping her tactical approach, and building the mental edge needed to compete against Egyptian players who have dominated the junior game for years.

The changes have been tangible. When they started working together, Singh relied heavily on her backhand. Under Ghosal's guidance, her forehand has become equally dangerous.

"The real fight was won before you stepped on court. The work you've put in made the difference. All the hammering and making fun to get your brain cells working, finally paid off."

— Saurav Ghosal, in his social media tribute to Singh

"She has a lot of skill and she's one of the few players in the women's game who can vary her play so much," Ghosal told myKhel earlier this year. "We're trying to make that variation as structured and as clinical as possible."

From Junior Prodigy to Olympic Contender

Singh's trajectory has been steep. She made her senior international debut for India at just 14 during the 2022 Commonwealth Games and won medals at the Asian Games by 16. Earlier this year, she won the Squash on Fire Open — her first bronze-level title — defended her Indian Open crown back-to-back, and broke into the world's top 20, becoming the youngest Asian ever to do so and surpassing Nicol David's previous record.

She also became the World Junior No. 1 before her title run in Canada. Her current senior world ranking of No. 20 places her firmly in the mix for Los Angeles 2028, where squash will make its Olympic debut.

Ghosal sees a clear path ahead. "Anahat has great potential and we believe she can be top 10 and remain a mainstay in the top 10," he said. "If she keeps putting in the work over the next three, five, seven or ten years, she's primed to win a lot for India on the world stage."

What It Means for Indian Squash

Singh's achievement surpasses Joshna Chinappa's runner-up finish at the World Juniors in 2005, which had stood as India's best showing at the event for over two decades. It also represents a broader shift: Indian squash has gone from non-competitive at the international level to producing a genuine world-beater in a sport that Egypt has treated as its private domain.

"Indian squash has gone from being not really competitive to being pretty competitive at the junior level and quite competitive at the senior level," Ghosal told RevSportz. "Now we've won one of the big, big things. It's definitely something that will hopefully be the match which lights the fire."

For the diaspora, the timing is significant. With squash entering the Olympics for the first time, there is finally a global stage where Indian squash can reach beyond the sport's traditional Commonwealth audience. Singh, mentored by the country's greatest player, represents that crossover moment.
nri_angle: With squash making its Olympic debut at LA 2028, Anahat Singh's rise gives the Indian diaspora a world-class athlete to rally behind on the global stage.
